title: Theory Base of Accounting
description: Class 11 Accountancy: GAAP and the basic accounting concepts (entity, going concern, cost, dual aspect, matching, prudence), accounting conventions and assumptions, accounting standards, IFRS, and cash vs accrual basis.

topics.title: GAAP and the Basic Accounting Concepts
topics.concept:
If every accountant recorded transactions in their own way, no two sets of books could be compared. To prevent this, accounting follows a common framework called GAAP — Generally Accepted Accounting Principles. GAAP is the set of rules, concepts and conventions that guide how transactions are recorded and reported. These are not laws of nature; they are agreed practices that have stood the test of time and are now widely accepted.

The principles are usually split into concepts (the basic assumptions on which records are built) and conventions (customs followed in preparing statements). Here are the foundation concepts:

  • Business Entity Concept — the business is treated as separate from its owner. The owner's personal cash and the business cash are different. This is why the owner's investment is recorded as capital (a liability of the business towards the owner) and withdrawals as drawings.
  • Money Measurement Concept — only transactions that can be expressed in money are recorded. The health of the managing director or the morale of staff, however important, is not recorded.
  • Going Concern Concept — the business is assumed to continue for the foreseeable future, not to close down soon. This is why assets are shown at cost (less depreciation), not at their break-up sale value.
  • Accounting Period Concept — the endless life of a business is split into fixed periods (usually one year) so that profit and position can be measured and reported regularly.
  • Cost Concept (Historical Cost) — an asset is recorded at the price actually paid for it, not at its market value. A building bought for Rs 10,00,000 stays at Rs 10,00,000 (less depreciation) even if the market price rises.
  • Dual Aspect Concept — every transaction has two aspects, a debit and a credit of equal amount. This is the basis of double-entry and of the accounting equation: Assets = Liabilities + Capital.

These six concepts are the bedrock; the next topic adds the matching, prudence and disclosure ideas that complete the framework.

examples.problem: Example 1: The owner brings Rs 1,00,000 of his own savings into the business. Which concept explains why this is recorded as the business's liability (capital)?
examples.solution:
Owner and business are separate.

  • The business entity concept treats the business as separate from the owner.
  • So money brought by the owner is owed back to him → capital (a liability of the business).
examples.answer: The business entity concept — the business is separate from the owner, so his investment is the firm's capital (a liability to him).

examples.problem: Example 2: A plot bought for Rs 5,00,000 is now worth Rs 8,00,000 in the market. At what value is it shown, and under which concept?
examples.solution:
Record at purchase price.

  • The cost concept records assets at the price actually paid.
  • So it stays at Rs 5,00,000, not Rs 8,00,000.
examples.answer: At Rs 5,00,000 (cost), under the cost (historical cost) concept.

examples.problem: Example 3: Why are assets shown at cost less depreciation rather than at their immediate sale value?
examples.solution:
The firm is not closing.

  • The going concern concept assumes the firm continues for the foreseeable future.
  • So assets are valued for continued use, not for a forced sale.
examples.answer: Because of the going concern concept — the firm is assumed to continue, so assets are valued for use, not for immediate sale.

recap:
• GAAP = generally accepted accounting principles (concepts + conventions) ensuring comparable records.
  • Concepts: business entity (firm separate from owner), money measurement (money items only), going concern (firm continues), accounting period (split into years), cost (record at price paid), dual aspect (Assets = Liabilities + Capital).

quiz.q: Treating the business as separate from its owner is the:
quiz.explanation: The business entity concept separates the firm from its owner.

quiz.q: Recording an asset at the price actually paid is the:
quiz.explanation: The cost (historical cost) concept records assets at purchase price.

topics.title: More Concepts, Conventions and Accounting Assumptions
topics.concept:
Beyond the foundation concepts, accounting follows several more principles and conventions that decide when to record income and how to present statements.

  • Revenue Recognition (Realisation) Concept — revenue is recorded when it is earned/realised (when goods are sold or services rendered), not necessarily when cash is received. A credit sale is income today even if cash comes next month.
  • Matching Concept — to find the correct profit, the expenses of a period are matched against the revenues of the same period. This is why we add outstanding expenses and subtract prepaid expenses while preparing final accounts.
  • Full Disclosure Convention — all material information must be fully disclosed so that statements are not misleading. Hence the notes and disclosures attached to accounts.
  • Convention of Conservatism (Prudence) — "anticipate no profit but provide for all possible losses." This is why we create a provision for doubtful debts and value stock at cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower.
  • Convention of Consistency — the same methods (e.g. of depreciation or stock valuation) are followed year after year, so results can be compared. A change is allowed only with disclosure.
  • Convention of Materiality — only items important enough to affect decisions need detailed treatment; trivial items (a stapler, a few erasers) can be treated as expense at once.
  • Objectivity Concept — records should be based on verifiable evidence (vouchers, bills), free from personal bias.

Out of all these, three are called the fundamental accounting assumptions (AS-1): Going Concern, Consistency, and Accrual. They are presumed to be followed; if any is NOT followed, the fact must be disclosed.

examples.problem: Example 1: Goods are sold on credit on 28 March; cash is received on 10 April. In which year is the sale recorded as revenue, and under which concept?
examples.solution:
Earned, not received.

  • Revenue recognition records income when goods are sold (earned), not when cash arrives.
  • So the sale is revenue of the year ending 31 March.
examples.answer: In the year of sale (ending 31 March), under the revenue recognition (realisation) concept.

examples.problem: Example 2: Closing stock costing Rs 50,000 has a net realisable value of Rs 45,000. At what value is it shown, and under which convention?
examples.solution:
Lower of cost or NRV.

  • Conservatism: provide for possible losses, value stock at the lower figure.
  • Lower of Rs 50,000 and Rs 45,000 is Rs 45,000.
examples.answer: At Rs 45,000 (lower of cost and net realisable value), under the convention of conservatism (prudence).

examples.problem: Example 3: Name the three fundamental accounting assumptions under AS-1.
examples.solution:
From the standard.

  • Going concern, consistency and accrual.

recap:
• Revenue recognition: record income when earned (sale), not when cash received. Matching: match a period's expenses with its revenues.
  • Conventions: full disclosure, conservatism/prudence (no profit anticipated, all losses provided; stock at lower of cost/NRV), consistency, materiality, objectivity.
  • Fundamental assumptions (AS-1): going concern, consistency, accrual.

quiz.q: Valuing stock at cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower, follows the convention of:
quiz.explanation: Conservatism (prudence) provides for possible losses, hence lower of cost/NRV.

quiz.q: The three fundamental accounting assumptions are going concern, accrual and:
quiz.explanation: AS-1 lists going concern, consistency and accrual.

topics.title: Accounting Standards, IFRS and the Systems of Accounting
topics.concept:
Concepts and conventions still leave some room for different treatments. To narrow this and make accounts uniform and comparable, professional bodies issue Accounting Standards (AS).

  • Accounting Standards are written policy documents issued by an authority (in India, the ICAI / the National Financial Reporting Authority) that lay down how particular items must be recognised, measured, presented and disclosed.
  • Need / objectives: to bring uniformity, improve reliability and comparability, reduce confusion and the chance of manipulation, and protect users.
  • IFRS (International Financial Reporting Standards) are global standards issued by the IASB so that company accounts are comparable across countries. India has converged its standards with IFRS in the form of Ind AS.

A second theory idea is the basis (system) of accounting — when a transaction is recorded:

BasisCash basisAccrual (mercantile) basis
Income recorded when…cash is actually receivedit is earned (whether or not received)
Expense recorded when…cash is actually paidit is incurred (whether or not paid)
Outstanding / prepaid itemsignoredfully adjusted
True profit?not accurateaccurate & recommended
Recognised by Companies Act?NoYes (mandatory for companies)

The accrual basis is the one required by the Companies Act and assumed by AS-1, because it matches revenues and expenses to the correct period and so shows the true profit. The cash basis is simple but unsuitable for most businesses. Together, GAAP, the standards and the accrual system give accounting its reliable, comparable theory base — the foundation for the recording you will now learn.

examples.problem: Example 1: State any two objectives of accounting standards.
examples.solution:
Why standards exist.

  • To bring uniformity in accounting practice.
  • To improve reliability and comparability of financial statements.
examples.answer: To bring uniformity in accounting practice and to improve the reliability and comparability of financial statements.

examples.problem: Example 2: Salary of Rs 10,000 for March is paid in April. Under the accrual basis, in which year is it an expense?
examples.solution:
When incurred.

  • Accrual records an expense when incurred, not when paid.
  • The salary relates to March, so it is March's expense (outstanding).
examples.answer: In the year it relates to (March / year ending 31 March) — it is treated as an outstanding expense under the accrual basis.

examples.problem: Example 3: What is the Indian name for accounting standards converged with IFRS?
examples.solution:
Convergence.

  • India's IFRS-converged standards are called Ind AS.
examples.answer: Ind AS (Indian Accounting Standards converged with IFRS).

recap:
• Accounting Standards (AS): written rules for recognition, measurement, presentation & disclosure → uniformity, reliability, comparability.
  • IFRS = global standards (IASB); India's converged version = Ind AS.
  • Cash basis: record on receipt/payment of cash. Accrual basis: record when earned/incurred — gives true profit, required by the Companies Act.

quiz.q: Global standards that make accounts comparable across countries are:
quiz.explanation: IFRS are international financial reporting standards issued by the IASB.

quiz.q: Under which basis is income recorded only when cash is received?
quiz.explanation: The cash basis records income and expenses only on actual receipt/payment of cash.

questions.q: GAAP stands for:
questions.explanation: GAAP = Generally Accepted Accounting Principles.

questions.q: The business is treated as separate from its owner under the:
questions.explanation: The business entity concept separates the firm from the owner.

questions.q: Only transactions measurable in money are recorded under the:
questions.explanation: The money measurement concept records only money-measurable items.

questions.q: Assets are shown at cost less depreciation because of the:
questions.explanation: Going concern assumes continuation, so assets are valued for use, not forced sale.

questions.q: Every transaction has two aspects of equal amount under the:
questions.explanation: Dual aspect is the basis of double entry: Assets = Liabilities + Capital.

questions.q: The accounting equation is:
questions.explanation: Assets = Liabilities + Capital, from the dual aspect concept.

questions.q: Recording revenue when goods are sold rather than when cash is received is the:
questions.explanation: Revenue recognition (realisation) records income when earned.

questions.q: Matching a period's expenses with its revenues is the:
questions.explanation: The matching concept matches expenses to the revenues of the same period.

questions.q: 'Anticipate no profit but provide for all possible losses' is the convention of:
questions.explanation: This is conservatism (prudence).

questions.q: Following the same methods year after year is the convention of:
questions.explanation: Consistency requires the same methods each year for comparability.

questions.q: Closing stock is valued at cost or net realisable value, whichever is:
questions.explanation: Prudence requires the lower of cost and NRV.

questions.q: The three fundamental accounting assumptions (AS-1) are going concern, accrual and:
questions.explanation: Going concern, consistency and accrual.

questions.q: Indian accounting standards converged with IFRS are called:
questions.explanation: India's IFRS-converged standards are Ind AS.

questions.q: Under the cash basis of accounting, an expense is recorded when:
questions.explanation: Cash basis records on actual payment of cash.

questions.q: The basis of accounting required by the Companies Act is the:
questions.explanation: Companies must use the accrual basis, which shows true profit.

questions.q: A proprietor uses business cash to pay his son's school fees and records it as a business expense. Which concept has he violated?
questions.explanation: Personal expenses are drawings, not business expenses — the entity concept keeps owner and firm separate.

questions.q: A firm values its building at the current market price of Rs 90 lakh instead of its Rs 60 lakh cost. This breaches the:
questions.explanation: Under the historical cost concept the asset must stay at its actual purchase price (less depreciation).

questions.q: A trader treats a credit sale of 28 March as income of the next year because cash came in April. The concept ignored is:
questions.explanation: Revenue is earned at the date of sale, so it belongs to the year of sale, not the year of receipt.

questions.q: Why does the matching concept require us to add outstanding salaries while preparing final accounts?
options: So the full expense of the period is matched against the period's revenue
questions.explanation: Matching pairs all expenses incurred in a period (paid or not) with that period's revenue to show true profit.

questions.q: A company creates a provision for doubtful debts even though no debtor has yet failed to pay. This reflects:
questions.explanation: Prudence provides for possible future losses in advance — anticipate losses, not profits.

questions.q: A firm changes its depreciation method every year to show whatever profit it likes. Which convention does this defeat?
questions.explanation: Consistency requires the same methods each year; arbitrary changes destroy comparability.

questions.q: Recording a Rs 40 stapler as an expense at once instead of depreciating it over years is justified by:
questions.explanation: Materiality lets trivial items be expensed immediately because they don't affect decisions.

questions.q: Which statement about the going concern concept is correct?
options: It assumes the firm will continue for the foreseeable future
It assumes the firm will close next month
questions.explanation: Going concern presumes continuation, which justifies cost-based (not break-up) valuation of assets.

questions.q: Under the cash basis, a business that sold heavily on credit but received little cash would report:
options: Understated profit, because credit sales are ignored until received
questions.explanation: Cash basis ignores credit sales until cash arrives, so profit is understated and inaccurate.

questions.q: If a firm does NOT follow one of the fundamental accounting assumptions, AS-1 requires that it:
questions.explanation: Going concern, consistency and accrual are presumed; any departure must be disclosed.
